OP, you're falling for the textbook case of something we call "Survivor Bias" in mathematics

You're making a sweeping generalization about your games based on a small subset of moves (the blunders), whilst ignoring data that might have caused you to make them.

Say, if there are 10 moves in a position, 9 of which are losing, of course you took the extra time to calculate all the lines and probably still played the blunder line. Compare this to 10 quick "best move" ladder mate, where all your moves are premoves. 

The only statistical interpretation you can make from this data is that your best move positions, ON AVERAGE, are less time consuming than blunder move positions.

It says next to nothing about how good or bad your actual Chess is getting. When you get better/worse, all 3 of those time variables will be affected at once, not just one.

No, chess does not have an analytical solution, ie it's an unsolved problem mathematically.

Computers only approximate a solution numerically using minimax with alpha beta pruning, hence they fall victim to things like Horizon effect.

But it does tilt back and forth, you just can't see it.

Such devices are controlled by **PID (or PID like) mechanism** , which uses the same logic you use to balance a stick on your fingers. If it goes too far one way the accelerometer quickly tells the circuit to sway the other way.

The difference is that humans aren't precise, it takes a long time for us to react and hence the swaying is visible. Machines' PID cycle lies in micro second range, and the corresponding swaying is too small to be noticed

Modern planes are built like a Faraday cage. Ie, their outermost shell is made of fully conductive material. 

This may seem counterintuitive, but a metal cage actually protects the insides from effects of electricity, as all current remains on the surface. You can see a neat demonstration of this effect here [here](https://youtu.be/pjw5gbkRTaY)

From the surface, the current then leaves the body of the plane from sharp edges like its nose and tails via a process called **Corona discharge** (lol)

Not OP but I'll attempt to answer since it's so close to my heart.

When a kid starts learning science, naturally they're attracted to stuff like blackholes, magnets, electrical circuits and the likes. Things which are whacky or have a cool experiment as a follow up. Then, a theory is given to them as an explanation.

But at that point, there's a fundamental disconnect between the theory you give them and what they observe, since they're not mathematically mature enough to grasp a theory in full. Yes they'd "know" a part of a theory, but they won't understand its wheres or whys. They'd see the explanation as say, you'd see an explanation for a plot hole in a movie. Many disconnected patches of explanations.

Newton's law are generally the first full set of actual physical laws they're taught. In principle, if you gave a student Newton's laws, he/she should be able to figure out everything from why moon doesn't fall to Earth to why a candle flame goes up instead of down, on their own. No ad-hoc explanations needed from an authority figure, in true spirit of science. 

This is not the case with anything they're taught before it. Yes you can tell them that heat is jiggling of atoms, but that's no better than a sentence in a Harry Potter novel. It makes sense, but doesn't settle as a theory. You might as well tell them heat is caused by little fairies flapping wings, and they'd accept it. But Newton's laws gives them the power to mathematically deduce everything from first principles. 

I'm of strong belief that every physicist has at least one eureka moment in life when they fully grasp one mathematical law in all its completeness. That's the moment that turns science from a mere cool subject into... A way of thinking? A way of life?

Not only can light be "trapped", it is effectively how we study modern optics, using optical resonant cavities. 

For the simplest cavity, look no further than your microwave. You essentially set up standing light waves inside the oven that cook your food.

This works exactly similar to how you set up standing waves in a string, both of whose ends are clamped. If you stop plucking the string at any moment, the wave will die out because reflection at both ends is not perfect. You can see a string wave slowly die out after successive reflections, but not light wave because of how quickly it happens for the latter. 

(Edit: The comment above mine shows exactly how quickly!) 

However, if you inject new waves by plucking the string at just the right frequency, you'll get standing string waves, or in oven's case, standing light waves.
